text: Jessamy Little, who founded the Cass Runners Club, a 100-plus person running group in London comprised of her business school classmates, suggests asking potential members what days, times, and locations work best with their schedules. Some groups may favor an early morning sweat sesh, while others may prefer meeting after work. “A recommendation for a newer club is to have two set running days,” Little says. “One during the week that is more focused on ‘getting it done’ and one on weekends that can have a more ‘fun and footloose’ vibe.” For Little’s group, the weekend runs were geared toward exploring new areas of the city.

If you have new people coming in, you can’t assume that they know the rules and guidelines. Communication needs to be all the time. Even though the group’s weather-proof policy may be well understood among current members, every time the skies get gloomy, the club blasts their social channels with reminders that the runs are still on. It also helps to communicate the planned route, distance, and pace in advance so that new members can plan their fuel and attire accordingly.

Initially, The San Francisco Road Runners Club, a 400-member nonprofit group founded in 2001, didn’t seek sponsorships. Instead, it built relationships with local races, running stores, and government entities, like the National Parks Service and the Department of Parks & Recreation. “We volunteered in local parks to help improve the areas we run,” say Lisa Griffin and Deb Holcomb, two of the club’s original founders. “We made (and still make) annual donations to the parks where we run. These days, many sponsors come to us. We seem to have a good reputation in the community.” Your group could also consider a charitable component that allows members to give back to worthy causes that impact the group—like covering hospital bills for someone’s sick family member, or donating money to replace possessions lost in a fire—through a fundraising run.

I heard that the best way to meet people is not just to be doing something at the same time but to be starting something at the same time. So first time moms groups, or adult art beginner classes. For running maybe you could specifically see if there are groups for first time marathon trainers or something. Something where there’s an actual reason to engage, share tips, etc people tend to be much more inclined to engage when they are new at an activity and others are in the same boat.

As someone who has been going to run clubs for 5 years now, and has been to at least over 15 of them now, I find that you tend to make the most friends when you focus on having fun, and choose to hang around the people who are having the most fun. From there, everything flows and happens naturally in my experience. It's all about not sweating the small stuff and doing what you gotta do. Whatever happens, happens. My favorite analogy is seeing it like this; people are like puzzle pieces. Some fit together so naturally that you barely even have to think about it. Then you have people who only fit together when you try really hard; to the point where they end up not even fitting all that great anyway. Then finally you have people who just don't click together no matter what you do. You'll know which people are which, as you spend time with them. Just remember that the goal isn't to be liked, but rather, to be YOU. To be yourself. From there, you will find your tribe, and your tribe will find you.

What I found to be effective was first consistently showing up to smaller/medium sized run clubs and then overtime gradually starting to talk to more and more people in that club and building rapport. I've found this more effective too because even if I do meet someone at a larger run club, sometimes they are only there for that one time, visiting, etc. and at that point you've lost any spark to run into that person again to try and form a consistent friendship. Whereas in a smaller club setting, there's a higher probability you'll encounter someone again since they live in the neighborhood or have some other reason for why they like going to the smaller/medium sized club.

I am a member of one of the bigger run clubs and I find it incredibly clique-y. I'm friendly with people at meetings and group runs but there's definitely a vibe that people are good with the cliques that they have formed and not looking to expand them. There's a new member run once a month that was very welcoming but after that you're pretty much on your own. The thing that rubs me wrong the most is that they organize valentines day notes to send to your running buddies in the club and it seems incredibly insular to me, but there's no organized activity to try to get people to mentor new members, organize pace cohorts for marathon training, or anything like that.

Mindset is the first issue that jumps out at me. If you keep telling yourself that your hobbies are solitary and that there are no opportunities, then you’ll never get out and meet anyone who is interested in the same thing. Why? Your brain will reject related opportunities because they don’t confirm your belief. But I can guarantee you that there are other folks interested in the same things as you. Go find them - check out the local library. Ask around. Go to a bar (you don’t have to drink) and chat people up. Take walks and see who ends up in your path - talk with them.

So practice socializing with friends or family or other people you know - this is Level 1. Then go into Level 2, where you have one stranger and one or two people you know, and get a little comfortable there. Then Level 3, where you have one person you know and a few you don’t. Then Level 4, where you meet a stranger but in a situation where you’re a little comfortable (your office or home or favorite hangout, for example). And Level 5 is where you meet one or two strangers in a strange place. Don’t go to Level 6 or 7 right away, where you talk to a large crowd of unknown people in a party, or speak in front of a crowd.

Besides the more obvious stuff like trail information and where and when to meet up, the itinerary should include what times you plan to begin and stop hiking each day, what locations you plan to make extended stops, and how fast you expect the group to travel in between planned stops. Build in as much flexibility as you can and be open to suggestions, but try to plan things so that the group stays together as much as possible. The group leader is ultimately responsible for the group and it's hard to have oversight if you have people splintering off and doing their own thing.

Any small and comfortable backpack will work. My husband will literally hike for miles with just a regular school backpack lol. I use one that’s smaller with padded shoulder straps and straps across the chest to help distribute weight because I am on the weaker side. For tools I only bring a pocket knife. Emergency kit I only use in remote areas on long hikes. They sell emergency kits on Amazon or REI. Anything with bandaids, gauze, antihistamines, anti inflammatories, ointment for bug bites, small scissors, etc.. When you get into longer and more difficult hikes there will be more gear needed for safety.

Great to hear you’re getting into hiking! For gear, running shoes can work for easy trails, but investing in proper hiking shoes is worth it for grip and ankle support. A lightweight, comfy backpack (20-30L) is ideal—make sure it has a chest strap for stability. Essentials to bring: plenty of water, snacks, sunscreen, a basic first-aid kit, and a rain jacket. As for things people don’t tell you: always check trail conditions and weather ahead of time, start early to avoid getting caught in the dark, and pace yourself—it’s okay to take breaks. Also, trails can be less “picturesque” than Instagram makes them seem, so embrace the journey, not just the destination! Have fun out there!

I began camping as an adult and now camp tons. My best advice would be to start super simple. Don't try to make grand Dutch oven meals, camp 20 miles into the backcountry and erect a tent from found materials. Don't try to run before you can walk! Buy a simple tent. Eat granola bars or instant oatmeal for breakfast. Lunch is sandwiches from the cooler (or skip the cooler and have peanut butter!). Dinner is hot dogs over the fire and chips. Got that down? Maybe buy a stove and heat up some canned chili next time. (Don't forget the can opener! Number one item I've loaned fellow campers of the years.) This advice also extends to your camp site. A state park campground not too far from a town would be ideal. Then, whatever you forget can be purchased and, if the weather is more than your gear can bear, you can hide out in a coffee shop, eat at a diner or even wander through a grocery store. Secondly, don't get too skimpy on the comfort stuff if you (or your friend) want to ever want to go again - sleeping pad, pillow, WARM whatever (hat, gloves, sweatshirt, blanket, sleeping bag).

In addition to the other tips I think there is something important to be aware of. You won't be able to control other people actions. There isn't a magic word to make people be on time. Even less for a hobby. Also as long as everyone else wait for them, people will keep being late. My advice, find the subreddit of your city. Post about finding people interested on boardgames, not once, every week or so. Reddit is fickle, sometime a post will vanish into oblivion and sometimes the same post may bloom. Regarless where you live, there's going to be gamers. Guaranteed. The key is to play with people that want to play. Don't wait for people that are an hour late, if they arrive late too bad, they can watch and learn the game while you play with those on time. Just enjoy the game with people that enjoy the game.

The biggest thing I will mention is that you need to make sure that people are on the same page and want the same thing. I have a group of friends that gets together to play games once a month. The majority of the group wants to play party games and talk in between turns. Knowing this, I don't bring any complex games, am flexible on when things start/end, and try to play games with large player counts (Incan Gold, Camel Up, social deduction games, Codenames). On the other hand, I have a completely separate group that I regularly organize sessions of 3 hour long, heavy games. Everyone comes in knowing what kind of game we're playing, does their research of learning the game ahead of the time via videos, and respects the fact that we have set starting and ending times.

I think it’s a good idea for you to try a bunch of different TYPES of games, so you figure out what you like and dislike. For example, engine builders, or dudes on a map, or worker placement. Also, you can go for themes that might interest you, like zombies, or superheroes, or the natural world. There are games that I love the theme of, but hate the gameplay. And of course, vice versa. On the other hand, some games are so good that I live it despite its flaws. for example the shitty art in Sentinels of the Multiverse, or the weird and mixed art style of Terraforming Mars. What are your interests outside games? Do you like sports, or fantasy stuff, or superheroes? Try games that fit into your interests, and then try the highly rated games (check boardgamegeek) in that genre.

For a beginner, a good list of extremely easy to find games that covers these kind of things to try at a cafe before you buy anything would be like: Quacks of Quedlinburg (push your luck, 'deck' building), Azul (drafting). Inis (dudes on a map) Railroad Ink (roll and write) and Welcome To (roll and write with less visualisation needed). The Crew (trick taking). Modern Art (auctioning) or Bohnanza (auctioning) - moving into Castles of Mad King Ludwig (building, auctioning). Sushi Go (pass and play). Codenames Duet (communication). Pandemic (cooperative) or maybe Dorfromantic (cooperative, not stressful). Sheriff of Nottingham (bluffing). Catan (real time strategy).

text: The placement of your initial settlements is very important. Your initial settlements (along with the first couple rounds of dice rolls) have a large impact on your game, affecting whether you get off to a quick start or lag behind. Some things to keep in mind when placing your initial settlements include: Probability of numbers: All else equal, a space bordering more dots is better than a space bordering fewer dots. Diversity of numbers: In general, starting with, e.g., 4-5-6-8-10-11 is going to give you an easier game than 4-4-6-6-10-11, since you will receive cards on more dice rolls, which then helps you build and/or trade more consistently, and helps you avoid having too many cards in your hand when a 7 is rolled. Mix of resources: All else equal, it's better to have direct access to more resources. Subpoint: In general, wheat is important at all stages of the game, sheep tend to be slightly worse than other resources (due to lower need and relative abundance). Note that the usefulness of resources changes as the game progresses.

As mentioned above, trick takers have strong-armed their way onto my list this year. Coincidentally, this one is also from Allplay. Piñatas is not the most flashy or innovative card game in this genre. But it has proven to be one of my favorite competitive trick takers for having a single brilliant twist. You’re out of the round when you win three tricks, and you immediately score points based on how many tricks other players have won. Crucially, the last player in the round effectively busts for waiting too long to go out and thus ends up with the worst score results. If you’ve ever been at a piñata party, then you may know what it feels like to be the last person in line to take a swing after that thing is already busted open and all the candy has spilled out. Piñatas is wonderfully punchy while staying squeaky clean in its execution. It’s not even all that new. This game is basically a perfect meld of Reiner Knizia’s wackier Voodoo Prince and tighter Marshmallow Test — two games that were already extremely similar. So hate this pick if you wish, but it’s technically a different game. Plus it features illustrated piñatas that get beaten to a pulp across the increasing card values.

I think also one of the inherent most difficult parts is finding both the right people and the right amount of people. Because multiplayer games are largely just up to 4 people, its really hard to find a group that is somehow small enough that you don't have too many people and now have to pick who to play with, but also don't get stuck with a small group that you don't actually vibe with. Like I'm sure I could find a massive gaming Discord server and join up and there would be dozens of people all playing all the time, but there will be so many people, nobody wants to be flexible and stay with the same people, they just play their game and that's it. Just like I could find a random person on Reddit and be like "hey we will just be friends now", but like what are the chances we actually will vibe long term?

The one course I play at, their league people are super friendly. When I was a brand new player, sometimes I would show up while they had something going on that I wasn't aware of, and they always said I could play through or tag along with a card if I wanted to. Play enough times at the same disc golf course, and you'll see some of the same people over and over again. Some people are self conscious about their skill level, and may turn you down if you ask to play. Some people just wanted to be alone and do their thing. Just like dating, you'll get yeses and nos. Ask enough times without being weird about it, and you'll find someone to throw discs with. Strike up conveersations about what discs people like throwing on certain holes of the course.

To not compare your abilities with others. The climbing gym can be pretty intimidating for someone new, so try just to focus on doing what looks fun or sounds fun without worrying about how you look in comparison to others. We all start out as beginners. I second this. The difference between two people's skill level their first time in the gym can be huge, some people climb v9 their first month, others are still struggling on v0. But if those two people climb 2x a week for 10 years they'll likely be climbing about the same level. If you find you "suck at climbing" your first day, congrats! That means you probably won't hit a plateau for a long time, you'll be moving up in the grades pretty consistantly for years.

You are going to hear "push with your feet! Don't pull yourself up with your hands, push yourself up the wall with your legs!" Or some variant a lot. I heard this a lot when I first started because I had a terrible tendancy to pull with my arms too much. I kept hearing people saying this but I didn't understand how to implement it. After a couple months of climbing it finally clicked. Twist your body to reach for a hold. Instead of pulling your body closer to the wall with your arms, twist your hips into the wall on one side to reach higher. So if you are trying to reach for a hold above you on your right, twist your hip to the right into the wall so that your right hip is close to the wall with your left hip away from the wall. Now you are closer to the hold and can reach it without pulling your body into the wall with your arms. You should rarely ever need to bend your elbows basically at all.

Yes, you show up with a paddle, hopefully some stable shoes that you won't roll your ankles in, then ask people where the beginners are and if someone could explain the rules to you such that you can mix in. You can also find That Pickleball Guy on YouTube that explains the rules. It's best to have a basic understanding of the game, like how to keep score and general court positioning before you go, but where there are beginners, they'll likely be friendly enough and excited enough to show you.

I’ve been organizing and hosting a local chapter of Silent Book Club for two and a half years. During this time, I’ve learned a lot about what works in attracting people to my club and keeping them coming—and what doesn’t work. I hope that this post about how to organize and host a book club will help you if you are curious about how to start a book club of your own. I also hope it will help you if you are a current Silent Book Club leader striving to keep the momentum going in your already existing club. Tip #1: Location, Location, Location. A variety of drink and food options (alcoholic and nonalcoholic options; healthy and not-so-healthy options; meat and vegetarian options). A welcoming, cozy atmosphere, without too much noise.

text: The most successful book club is the one that suits the group. If you want to set up a book club, find a group of people and figure out what works for you. You don't have to meet every month, you don't have to read particular books, you don't even have to have set rules (maybe one month you read poetry and twenty people come, the next month you read a horror and only four people are interested etc)! People will be more engaged if they don't feel they're being put out by 'rules', so make sure everyone agrees on the boundaries. I often find that hard and fast rules like size limits, genre, completion etc can be off-putting to people, and some flexibility can make your group more accessible. If you want to join a book club, decide what you want out of it and find a group that fits. It might take a few goes, and that's okay! If you can't find one that fits, make one!

I work in a bookshop and my book clubs run through that, so perhaps slightly different to other clubs. For me personally, it means I am in 'work mode' and slightly less relaxed, but I think making them virtual while the shop has been closed has actually made the group closer/made it feel more relaxed. Unexpected side effect! For both we have a 'hat' (for one of them we use a physical hat when we meet in person) - people add suggestions and we random draw to select the next read. My sci-fi club is a little more casual - sometimes we pick a few and vote on them, or decide collectively that we want something specific - eg a lighter read after doing something heavy, a horror book for Halloween, a shorter book when a meeting is postponed. And then go from there! I really love both book clubs, and I think during lockdown the members have really appreciated our monthly catch ups!

I would have a list of questions ready but open the conversation asking if someone has something they'd like to begin with. If no one does or they're too shy then bring up the questions you've prepared. If you're having a hard time thinking of some, google general book discussion questions or questions specific to the book. For the awkwardness of beginning and introductions try to think of something fun. Maybe everyone can introduce themselves as their favorite book or genre? Introducing yourself first and making it fun may help everyone else feel more comfortable. Assuming this is a book club of all adults if there's a conversation hog you notice after a while you can privately address it with them. Or during the meeting just ask others directly what they think of what person A said. That way you're including others back into the conversation. Don't put too much pressure on yourself though. This sounds like it's supposed to be a fun casual thing so just focus on that, having fun. You can always ask the others their opinions on how they would like to see the book club ran. Happy reading!

Fun group cooking activties include: Vietnamese salad rolls. Someone with great knife skills can do the matchstick carrots and cucumber; someone else can shell, devein, and cook shrimp; etc. Everyone can fill and roll their own rice paper wrappers with what they want. Lasagna rolls baked in muffin tins -- same idea as salad rolls, where everyone can build their lasagna the way they want, with red sauce or white, meat or not, kind of cheese, etc. Korean bo ssam -- Martha Stewart has simple instructions and a great video. You cook the pork roast and lay out side dishes like bean sprout salad, smashed cucumber salad, etc., make sauces (see link above), and everyone puts together their own lettuce wraps.

You should also make sure that the recipe consists of steps that are easy to divide up. After all, everyone has a job to do. A dish with lots of ingredients that need to be prepared is ideal. Measuring spices, washing salad, paring meat or chopping vegetables. The individual tasks, which may seem a little tedious on their own, make cooking together interesting. Then a quick curry with rice or a colourful bowl becomes an absolute turbo dish. In the following recipe gallery you will find our Blitz favourites, which are even quicker to put on the table when you work as a team. The division of labour is just as important as the division of tasks. Vegetables can be chopped at the dining table, but the person who washes the salad has to go to the sink. It is also important to make sure that everyone really does stay together and that nobody moves to another room for reasons of space. Perhaps the coffee machine can be moved off the worktop and maybe the bar table will still fit in the kitchen?

But let's not forget the first option: the raucous fun-fest! Cooking in groups provides plenty of opportunity to: Take on a project you might not be so eager to embark on as an individual: Timpano, dumplings, baked Alaska. Assign different members of your groups certain tasks. Then be each other's helpers! Start a dish that you might make by yourself but that will be made so much easier by the help of others to chop, husk, mince, or mash. Accommodate preferences by making something customizable, so that your fellow group members can leave out what they don't like (and add more of what they do like). Bond with friends!

I just recently got back into collecting Pokémon cards with the 151 set myself. It totally depends on what your personal preferences are and what you want to achieve at the end. If you want a clear goal and cohesion (and want to crack some boosters in the process): try to collect a complete base set (one of every card in a set excluding all those secret rares and special illustration rares). Its also doable in a reasonable timeframe without being too expensive depending on the cards. It is also a satisfying process to fill up those empty spots in a binder. Buying an ETB from one of the most recent sets that appeals the most to you might be a good starting point; you get a storage box for your cards and some sleeves with it. Having some additional penny sleeves at hand is also never wrong in my opinion. A Playmat is nice to have ( a large mousepad would work just the same) but a clean surface is probably enough to lay out the cards since you probably wont grate them across the whole table/floor.

Like most TCGs, Pokémon is an incredibly versatile game, and there’s no single best way to have fun with it. Your answer will shape what you buy, how you store cards, and how quickly you expand your collection. Collecting For Duels: For some, collecting Pokémon cards is all about the thrill of demolishing your opponent in a duel. Collecting to Invest: Pokémon cards as a financial investment really took off during the pandemic, with booster box prices reaching the thousands in some cases. Just remember that condition, rarity, demand, and timing all matter, so avoid treating every card as a guaranteed investment. Collecting for a Good Time: This category describes the vast majority of collectors. Pokémon card collecting as a casual hobby has been around for decades now. As far as TCGs go, Pokémon is relatively easier to get into than something like MTG. Additionally, the visually stunning artwork from new lineups like Twilight Masquerade and Temporal Forces is doing a great job of pulling new collectors into the hobby. If you’re collecting for fun, choose sets, characters, or card art that make you excited to keep opening, trading, and organizing your collection.

If you’re fishing structure like brush piles, docks, or standing timber, especially in water deeper than 5 feet, it’s hard to beat the slip float rig. Unlike fixed floats, a slip float allows you to set the depth with a bobber stop, giving you precise vertical control. That’s critical, because crappie don’t like to feed down — they want the bait above them, where they can see and rise to it. Use a small wire Aberdeen hook, typically a #2 or #4, which lets you hook the minnow through the lips or behind the dorsal (both of which are viable depending on your setup). Crappie have delicate mouths, so a thin-wire hook reduces tearing. And because these hooks bend out under pressure, they’re forgiving when fishing snag-prone structures. The key to optimizing this rig is subtlety. Use light fluorocarbon or mono in the 4- to 6-pound range to maximize sensitivity. Avoid over-weighting the float; you want just enough split shot to keep the minnow down, but not so much that its natural movements are restricted. You’re not trying to force a reaction strike; you’re simply putting dinner on the plate and waiting for the bite.

I do it a couple ways. You can use one of the fishing apps like fishbrain to see the general locations where people are catching fish. I tend to open up my maps app when im bored, look for blue that i havent fished at, and usually go to it at some point. Ill always save the spots on my actual map (a star will remain) that i think could be good spots to fish. Even small creeks and tributaries can be a fun walk and discovery. A lot of smaller creeks can still have nice fishable pockets in them. Look for sharp bends or areas with steep terrain on one side and flat on the other. Make sure not to trespass when exploring for new water. Even larger obvious fishing bodies like lakes, reservoirs, and rivers will still need exploring. All parts of these bodies are not created equal.

Respecting the catch is an important conservation ethic. Fish should never be wasted. If you catch a fish that is under the legal or minimum size or that you do not want to keep, release it quickly. Here are three tips to make sure the fish you release has the best chance at surviving. Keep fish as wet as possible. Fish have a natural mucus layer that protects them in the water. Wet your hands or use wet rubberized gloves and a rubber net to handle the fish. Minimize airtime. Keep fish underwater as long as possible while removing the hook, getting ready for a photo, or preparing to release. If the fish has swallowed the hook, do not tear the hook out. Simply cut the line as close to the mouth as possible. You can revive a fish by gently moving it back and forth in the water so that water runs through its gills. When it begins to move around and can swim normally, let it go.

How many bars are you looking at going too and what time? You have a meet up place, maybe a park or small outdoor area nearby. I would message the agenda to everyone. A lot about 30 mins per bar. 1 drink. Then after 4 or 5 bars, you can all pick your favorites and go back, or end at what you know is going to be your vibe and enjoy your night . Trying to coordinate that many people after 4 or 5 bars becomes stressful, so I wouldn't make it longer than that, for the "organized" part.

This is a class from the Crafty Chica art retreat, people loved it! Watercoloring in a group is not only fun but relaxing. Water is fluid, the colors organically blend with each other, making each piece look beautiful and dreamy. A lot of people shy away from painting or drawing because they feel they aren’t good enough. But if you set it up in a class setting for your friends and allow for everyone’s creativity, you end up with amazing pieces with different looks. You’ll see that people will share ideas and encouragement! It’s truly incredible, so beautiful and see how proud everyone is of their pieces! Yes, you can totally host a painting party at a restaurant! Call ahead to save the space and have everyone pay for their meals but- what a great idea right?! Grab some ornaments like Kathy did for this event and bring paints. Again, everyone is enjoying the conversation and fellowship while they make their own unique creations!
